name: IAC 2023 Delhi Winner
author: Arne Jach
why: Built to tame a wild pineapple-fermented coffee: cool water and almost no agitation keep funky fruit pleasant instead of harsh. Made for anaerobic and co-fermented lots like your Yelnoorkhan.

name: WAC 2023 Champion
author: Tay Wipvasutt
why: A split dose adds a late burst of fresh aromatics on top of a sweet base. Best with expressive fruity beans.

name: IAC 2022 Bengaluru
author: Shruti Vashist
why: A long, slow immersion of a medium-dark coffee builds body with a light acidity — good for chocolaty and nutty Indian estate coffees.

name: IAC 2022 Champion
author: Pratik Sharma
why: Two temperatures: a hotter bloom for sweetness, a cooler main pour to keep acidity crisp. Suits Indian light roasts with fruit or citrus notes.

name: WAC 2022 Champion
author: Jibbi Little
why: Removing chaff and fines strips out bitterness and muddiness for maximum clarity — rewards bright, clean citrus and floral coffees.

name: WAC 2021 Champion
author: Tuomas Merikanto
why: Designed to avoid harsh, tannic sourness in a complex light roast: 80 °C and minimal agitation. Ideal for delicate, floral, high-acidity beans.

name: WAC 2021 Runner-up
author: Maru Mallee
why: A firm stir and a long steep at 93 °C extract plenty of sweetness; the swirl after flipping keeps it even. A sweet, full cup from fruity or honey beans.

name: Championship Cold Water Bypass
author: Alexander Mills
why: Quick, strong and diluted with hot and room-temperature water — sweet, balanced and drinkable straight away. A forgiving pick for caramel and nutty mediums.

name: Citric Sweet
author: Rama Marti
why: A slow, gentle pour and stopping the press early keep clean citric brightness balanced by sugar sweetness — made for a washed Colombian.

name: WAC 2019 Champion
author: Wendelien van Bunnik
why: Lots of coffee and only 40 s of contact pulls sweetness fast without bitterness, then it's cooled so sweetness reads loud. Great for juicy, sweet beans.

name: WAC 2019 Runner-up
author: Benja Khemacheva
why: High dose, hot water and a pre-bypass make a round, heavy, sweet cup. Handles fruity naturals and caramel-sweet mediums well.

name: Love me some acid
author: Kata Muhel
why: Low 81 °C and a gentle swirl are designed to make acidity sing. Pick this when your bean tastes of lemon, berries or flowers.

name: WAC 2018 Champion
author: Carolina Ibarra Garay
why: An extreme 35 g concentrate topped up with hot and room-temperature water — dense sweetness and body. Best with sweet naturals and honey-process beans.

name: WAC 2018 Runner-up
author: Xiaobo Zhang
why: Low 80 °C and a coarse grind keep it bright and clean, with a sprinkle of fines for body. Suits delicate, fruity light roasts.

name: WAC 2018 Third Place
author: Evgeni Pinchukov
why: Low dose, low temperature and an early stop to the press — a light, tea-like cup for bright washed coffees.

name: WAC 2017 Champion
author: Paulina 'Panda' Miczka
why: Built on a Kenyan AA. A strong concentrate diluted afterwards keeps the vivid citrus and blackcurrant while staying sweet.

name: WAC 2017 Runner-up
author: Yusuke Narisawa
why: Two paper filters and a coarse grind make an exceptionally clean cup; the pinch of fines adds body back. Clarity-first, so delicate florals and fruit shine.

name: WAC 2016 Champion
author: Filip Kucharczyk
why: A huge dose brewed short, then diluted: lots of sweetness and body without bitterness. Makes juicy, syrupy cups from fruity and honey-process beans.

name: WAC 2015 Champion
author: Lukas Zahradnik
why: Cool water plus a hard stir, built on a washed Kenyan: bright blackcurrant and citrus with sweetness but no harshness.

name: WAC 2015 Runner-up
author: Nick Hatch
why: Moderate temperature and a long, slow 60 s press give a balanced, sweet cup. A good all-rounder for light-medium beans with fruit and sugar notes.

name: WAC 2014 Champion
author: Shuichi Sasaki
why: Very low 78 °C water and stopping before the dregs avoid bitterness completely, so floral and citrus notes stand out. Too gentle for chocolaty beans — they taste flat.

name: WAC 2012 Champion
author: Charlene De Buysere
why: No stirring, a short bloom and a press that stops early keep the cup clean and sweet. A gentle method that won't strip a light, bright bean's fruit.

name: A Fruity Perspective
author: Div
why: Coaxes fruit out of medium and medium-dark beans — a long, heavy steep that brings dark fruit out alongside chocolate.

name: AeroPress Vietnamese Iced Coffee
author: AeroPress
why: Built for robusta: heavy, bitter-chocolate coffee that stands up to sweet condensed milk and ice.
kw: vietnamese viet vietnam ca phe sua da cà phê sữa đá condensed milk robusta phin sweet iced official

name: AeroTonic
author: Clem InTheCoffee
why: Tonic is bitter and citrusy, so bright beans pair best — lemon, berry and floral notes turn into a sparkling coffee spritz. Very roasty beans can taste medicinal with tonic.
kw: tonic espresso tonic coffee tonic spritz sparkling fizzy soda mixer lemon lime

name: Alan Adler Cold Brew
author: Alan Adler
why: Cold water pulls sweetness and body but very little acidity. Chocolaty, nutty beans taste smooth and sweet; bright fruity ones taste flat.

name: Alan Adler Original
author: Alan Adler
why: The inventor's original: cool 80 °C water and a fast press keep bitterness low on everyday darker roasts. Smooth and low-acid from chocolaty and nutty beans.

name: Blue Bottle
author: Blue Bottle Coffee
why: A vigorous stir at 1:00 and fuller extraction give a round, sweet, medium-bodied cup — the classic for balanced medium roasts.

name: Coffee Collective Brew Guide
author: Coffee Collective (Elliot Stølegaard)
why: Coffee Collective roasts light and fruity; a short sealed steep with a second stir keeps clarity while building sweetness.

name: Coffee with April
author: April Coffee
why: A low dose and cooler 88 °C water make a light, juicy, low-bitterness cup — designed for Kenyan and Ethiopian coffees.

name: EVP's Iced Coffee
author: Peter (EVP Coffee)
why: A medium-dark Colombian over ice gives a smooth, cold-brew-like but syrupy cup — chocolaty and caramel beans taste best.
kw: iced smooth cold brew style syrupy colombian medium dark

name: Hoffmann AeroPress for Milk Drinks
author: James Hoffmann
why: A 1:5 concentrate made to carry milk. Chocolaty and nutty beans keep their flavour under milk; light fruity ones disappear or turn sour.

name: Hoffmann Iced AeroPress
author: James Hoffmann
why: Brewed hot and flash-chilled on ice, which locks in aromatics — iced coffee that still tastes of fruit and flowers, not flat cold brew.

name: Hoffmann Ultimate (original, 99 °C)
author: James Hoffmann
why: A lean ratio and near-boiling water extract fully without stirring — a clear, tea-like cup that shows off delicate light roasts.

name: Lance Hedrick — A Very Good Recipe
author: Lance Hedrick
why: Built to cut bitterness and astringency with a gentle press — a safe, balanced recipe for medium beans with caramel and nut notes.

name: Lance Hedrick — Dark Roast & Decaf
author: Lance Hedrick
why: Very cool water and a coarse grind on dark, decaf or aged coffee keep the chocolate and roast and drop the ashy bitterness.

name: Lance Hedrick — Light Roast Concentrate
author: Lance Hedrick
why: Designed to cut woody, vegetal notes from light roasts and boost acidity and body — makes fruity light roasts taste juicy.

name: Market Lane
author: Huw @ Market Lane (Market Lane Coffee)
why: A simple steep where more stirring makes a stronger cup — easy to tune to a fruity or sweet bean.

name: On the Road with Stumptown
author: Stumptown Coffee Roasters
why: Hot water and two stirs make a full, sweet, hearty cup — great for chocolaty, nutty and caramel beans, and travel-proof.

name: Ralf Rüller Personal
author: Ralf Rüller
why: Aimed at a juicy cup with a creamy mouthfeel: fruity beans get their juiciness, honey-process beans their sweetness.

name: Sightglass Coffee
author: Devan Holt (Sightglass Coffee)
why: Fine grind and hot water extract fast — a sweet, well-rounded cup in about a minute. Works with most beans; best with caramel-sweet mediums.

name: Tetsu Kasuya Pour-Over
author: Tetsu Kasuya
why: Percolation like a V60 rather than immersion — clean and bright, for floral and citrusy light roasts.

name: Tim Wendelboe
author: Tim Wendelboe
why: Short steep, precise stirring, light ratio. Tim Wendelboe roasts very light, and this recipe is built to show clean floral and fruity acidity.

name: Tim Wendelboe, Stronger
author: Tim Wendelboe
why: A moka-style strong cup from espresso-roasted coffee — dense, chocolaty and roasty. Too intense for light fruity beans.

name: Tyler's Bypass
author: Tyler Duncan (Topeca Coffee)
why: Skimming the oils off, cupping-style, gives a very clean cup that shows delicate florals and stone fruit — made for an Ethiopian Guji.

name: AeroPress Espresso
author: Coffee Lovers TV
why: A short, hot, hard extraction. Dark, chocolaty beans give a thick espresso-like shot; light beans turn sour.

name: AeroPress Iced Latte
author: Mark C
why: Built on Indian Monsooned Malabar — low-acid, heavy and chocolaty, exactly what iced milk needs. Great for your Truffle Twilight.

name: Flash Brew Iced Coffee
author: Marc Werle
why: Flash-brewed hot onto ice to keep a light roast's character with little dilution — the iced choice for bright, fruity beans.
kw: flash brew iced japanese style hot onto ice light

name: Freddo Espresso
author: Minas Pitsos
why: A long-steeped light-to-medium concentrate shaken with ice — sweet, frothy and bright. Fruity and caramel beans keep their sweetness when chilled.
kw: freddo greek shaken frothy iced espresso summer

name: Fresh Orange Iced Coffee
author: Victor Bacega
why: Orange and a hard shake make a frothy, citrusy iced coffee. Fruity beans go orange-berry; chocolaty beans make a chocolate-orange.
kw: orange citrus fruit shaken shaker frothy iced experimental

name: Fruity Press
author: Yker Valerio
why: Made for natural and honey-process medium roasts; a rest after pressing opens up aroma and sweetness.

name: Fuller Flavour Vietnamese Style
author: Thien Le
why: A 9-minute steep builds the heavy body of a phin brew; made for robusta-heavy or dark blends that stand up to condensed milk.
kw: vietnamese viet vietnam ca phe sua nong cà phê sữa nóng condensed milk robusta arabica blend long steep hot egg coconut palm sugar ginger

name: Greek Freddo Espresso
author: Serafeim Davranis
why: Built on a light Ethiopian for a sweet, tangy freddo. Shaking adds froth, and the cold makes fruit taste crisp.
kw: freddo greek shaken frothy iced espresso ethiopia summer

name: Hello Darkness, My Old Friend
author: Peter Do
why: Low temperature and a low dose made for dark roasts — balances bitterness and acidity for a smooth daily dark cup.

name: Iced Americano
author: Carl Miranda
why: Hoffmann's method pressed onto ice — clean and sweet. The author uses a guava-noted mild roast; fruity and caramel beans suit it.

name: Iced Brown Sugar Oat Shaken Aeropresso
author: Michael Gordon
why: Brown sugar, cinnamon and oat milk love caramel and nutty beans. The author also found light roasts work, adding a fruity lift.
kw: brown sugar cinnamon oat milk shaken starbucks copycat sweet iced syrup

name: Iced Coconut AeroPress
author: Yunus Yanin
why: Coconut water is mildly sweet and nutty — it pairs with nutty, chocolaty and caramel beans, like a coconut chocolate bar. Very acidic beans can taste sour against it.
kw: coconut water tropical iced mixer quick

name: Jonathan Gagné 10-Minute
author: Jonathan Gagné
why: Very high extraction — fine grind, boiling water, 9 minutes. Dense light roasts turn sweet and complex; darker roasts would go bitter.

name: Orange AeroPress Coffee
author: giii_muu
why: Brewed through an orange slice. The author asks for beans with bright acidity, so citrusy coffee and orange amplify each other.
kw: orange citrus fruit filter slice iced juice mixer experimental

name: Rule of Thirds
author: Tyler Laseter
why: A neutral, balanced recipe the author uses to taste every new coffee — a good first brew for an unfamiliar bag.

name: Spanish Latte
author: phbrewer
why: Condensed milk adds caramelised sweetness. The author uses a nutty, brown-sugar medium roast — nutty and caramel beans taste like dulce de leche.
kw: spanish latte condensed milk sweet creamy nutty brown sugar iced

name: Sweet, Bright and Iced!
author: Shy Foreman
why: Made for a natural light roast at 99 °C and pressed over ice — keeps the sweetness and juicy acidity the name promises.
kw: iced natural light bright sweet juicy

name: The AeroPress Flat White
author: European Coffee Trip
why: The author suggests an African natural — berry sweetness in milk tastes like strawberry-chocolate. Chocolaty beans work just as well.

name: The Only AeroPress Recipe You'll Ever Need
author: The Coffee Compass
why: A long, sealed steep with near-boiling water — full extraction and sweetness, smooth and forgiving. Good for everyday nutty and caramel beans.

name: V60 Style AeroPress (dark roast)
author: u/skelathon0703
why: Cooler water and a concentrate diluted afterwards keep a dark roast's chocolate while avoiding ash.

name: V60 Style AeroPress (light roast)
author: u/skelathon0703
why: Short, no-stir and V60-like — highlights delicate florals and citrus in light roasts.

name: Vietnamese Iced Coffee (Cà Phê Sữa Đá)
author: Steven Le
why: A small, strong dark-roast concentrate with condensed milk — smoky, chocolaty espresso roasts like your Truffle Twilight fit perfectly.
kw: vietnamese viet vietnam ca phe sua da cà phê sữa đá condensed milk sweet iced smoky dark
